lesson.title: Top to Bottom: Reading Peak-to-Peak Off a Scope Trace
lesson.summary: Peak-to-peak value spans the full vertical distance a waveform covers, from its highest instantaneous point to its lowest, and it is usually the very first number read off an oscilloscope trace.
lesson.body:
Peak-to-peak value, written Vpp or Ipp, is the total vertical span of a waveform: the difference between its highest instantaneous value and its lowest instantaneous value. For a symmetric sinusoid with no DC offset, the waveform swings up to +Vm and down to -Vm, so the peak-to-peak value is simply Vpp = Vm - (-Vm) = 2Vm, exactly double the peak value covered in the previous chapter.

Peak-to-peak is often the most natural quantity to read directly off an oscilloscope screen, because the scope shows you the full trace at once, and counting vertical divisions from the very top of the trace to the very bottom gives Vpp in one glance, with no need to first locate where zero volts sits on the display. Converting that reading into RMS or peak value for calculations comes afterward, but the raw measurement people actually make with their eyes is peak-to-peak.

Using the household outlet example from the previous chapter, where the peak value was found to be Vm = 169.71 V, the peak-to-peak value is Vpp = 2 times Vm = 2 times 169.71 = 339.42 V. That is the full vertical excursion the voltage covers every single cycle, from its highest point near +169.71 V to its lowest point near -169.71 V, a span of nearly 340 V even though the outlet is only rated at 120 V RMS.

Peak-to-peak becomes more interesting once a DC offset is present, because it is no longer just double the peak value. Suppose an oscilloscope trace shows a sinusoid riding on a DC bias, swinging from a maximum of +9 V down to a minimum of -3 V. The peak-to-peak value is the difference between those two extremes, Vpp = 9 - (-3) = 12 V. The amplitude of the oscillation, half of that span, is 12/2 = 6 V, and the DC offset sitting at the midpoint between the two extremes is (9 + (-3))/2 = 3 V. Notice that the peak value here, 9 V, is not half of 12 V, precisely because the waveform is not centered on zero.

That last example is the reason peak-to-peak, rather than peak value alone, is often the safer quantity to quote for a general waveform: it needs no assumption about where the signal is centered. Peak value tells you the single highest point reached; peak-to-peak tells you the full range covered, and for the plain, zero-centered sinusoids that dominate introductory AC analysis, the two are related by nothing more complicated than a factor of two.

There is also a direct shortcut from RMS to peak-to-peak for a sinusoid, without computing the peak value as a separate step: Vpp = 2 sqrt(2) Vrms. Applying it to the same 120 V RMS outlet gives Vpp = 2 times 1.41421 times 120 = 339.41 V, matching the 339.42 V found earlier by doubling the peak value, the tiny difference explained by rounding sqrt(2) along the way. In practice, a noisy or jittery signal can also make peak-to-peak measurements unreliable, since a single stray spike can inflate the reading well beyond what the underlying signal actually does, which is why lab instruments often report an RMS value alongside peak-to-peak, since RMS naturally averages out brief noise excursions that a peak-to-peak reading cannot ignore.
